title: Syllogism: Possibility Cases and Venn Diagram Mastery

questions.question: When is a possibility conclusion considered true?
options: Only when it holds in every valid Venn arrangement
When it is not definitely contradicted by the statements
Only when it matches real-world knowledge
When at least two arrangements support it
questions.rationale: The golden rule: a possibility is true when it is not definitely contradicted — you only have to fail to disprove it. Demanding truth in every arrangement is the standard for definite conclusions, not possibilities.

questions.question: Statement: All A are B. Conclusion: Some B being A is a possibility. What is the verdict?
options: False, because the statement only talks about A
True, because nothing is contradicted
False, because no A can be a B
True only if A is empty
questions.rationale: Nothing in 'All A are B' contradicts some B being A — in fact some B are A is definite here, and a definite truth always satisfies a possibility. The conclusion is true.

questions.question: Statement: Some A are not B. Conclusion: All A being B is a possibility. What is the verdict?
options: True, because some A may still be in B
False, because the statement directly contradicts it
True, because some never excludes all
Neither true nor false without more statements
questions.rationale: The statement itself says some A lie outside B, so the picture where all A are inside B is directly contradicted. The possibility fails.

questions.question: Statement: Some A are B. Conclusion: All A being B is a possibility. What is the verdict?
options: True, because some never excludes all
False, because some means not all
False, because all statements convert
True only when A and B are equal
questions.rationale: In formal logic 'some' only guarantees 'at least one' and never means 'not all', so the arrangement where circle A sits fully inside B still satisfies 'some A are B'. The possibility is true.

questions.question: Which statement type has NO valid conversion?
options: All A are B
Some A are B
No A is B
Some A are not B
questions.rationale: The O-type, 'Some A are not B', has no valid conversion — 'Some B are not A' does not follow from it. This single fact settles many trap options instantly.

questions.question: What is the valid conversion of 'All A are B'?
options: All B are A
Some B are A
No B is A
Some B are not A
questions.rationale: From 'All A are B' you may conclude 'Some B are A' by conversion. 'All B are A' is the classic invalid reversal.

questions.question: What is the recommended strategy for three-statement syllogisms?
options: Treat all three statements as one large statement
Combine the statements in pairs, then combine the derived conclusions
Check only the first and last statements
Convert every statement before reading the conclusions
questions.rationale: Derive every two-statement conclusion the rules allow, then treat those derived conclusions as new statements and combine again — like chaining A to B to C to D.

questions.question: Statements: Some chairs are tables. Conclusions: I. All chairs are tables. II. Some chairs are not tables. What follows?
options: Only I follows
Only II follows
Either I or II follows
Neither I nor II follows
questions.rationale: Neither conclusion follows definitely, but I and II form an A-O complementary pair on the same terms — one universal affirmative, one particular negative — so exactly one holds in every arrangement: either I or II follows.

questions.question: Statements: No cup is a plate. Some plates are dishes. Conclusion I: Some dishes being cups is a possibility. Does it follow?
options: No, because no cup is a plate
Yes, because dishes may sit outside the plate circle and overlap cups
No, because dishes are not mentioned with cups
Yes, because some cups are always dishes
questions.rationale: Dishes can overlap the cup circle anywhere outside 'plate' without violating 'No cup is a plate', so the possibility is not contradicted and is true. The definite claim 'Some cups are dishes', however, would not follow.

questions.question: Statements: Some emails are letters. All letters are posts. Conclusion I: Some emails are posts. Conclusion II: Some posts being letters is a possibility. What follows?
options: Only I follows
Only II follows
Both I and II follow
Neither follows
questions.rationale: I follows because Some + All combines to Some emails are posts. II also holds: 'Some posts are letters' is actually definite by conversion of 'All letters are posts', and a definite truth always satisfies a possibility.
